title: Second Chunce

jokes.text: Andy mowed the lawn at 2:00 in the morning due to jet lag
jokes.setup: April explains Andy has jet lag and they're on totally different schedules
jokes.punchline: His jet-lag behavior manifests as mowing the lawn at 2AM — a specific, absurd, and very Andy-appropriate choice of activity
jokes.explanation: The gag is perfectly character-specific — of all the disruptive jet-lag things Andy could do, lawn mowing at 2AM is hilariously on-brand: outdoorsy, loud, oblivious to others. The specificity elevates it above a generic 'he does dumb things' joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have jet lag so bad, I mowed the lawn at 2 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: At 2 in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The neighbors loved it.

jokes.text: Andy sleep-talks: 'That's my spaghetti, Chewbacca.'
jokes.setup: April tries to wake Andy up, who is deeply asleep
jokes.punchline: His sleep-talking reveals an absurd dream involving spaghetti and Chewbacca
jokes.explanation: An almost perfect six-word joke. The combination of 'spaghetti' and 'Chewbacca' is maximally random yet feels utterly authentic to Andy's brain. The possessive 'That's MY spaghetti' adds territorial urgency to the absurdity. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, and could only come from this character. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He fell asleep during sex. I just laid there thinking, 'Well, this is a new low.' But then I realized... I was kind of into it. Phrasing.

jokes.text: Andy sleep-calls the dog 'Champion' while passed out, then immediately crashes back down
jokes.setup: April is exasperated trying to keep Andy awake
jokes.punchline: Andy rouses just enough to interact with the dog by name, then collapses again — a visual beat showing how instantly he drops
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny moment — Andy is so out of it he can only mumble the dog's name before crashing. Works as physical comedy and reinforces the escalating jet-lag gag.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: May the forks be with you... I love you, spaghetti...

jokes.text: April was about to spray Andy with a hose inside the house; Andy's response: 'I kinda want you to do it now.'
jokes.setup: Andy catches April holding a garden hose inside the house, ready to use it on him
jokes.punchline: Instead of being alarmed, Andy's groggy enthusiasm reverses — he now WANTS to be hosed
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is sharp: we expect Andy to object to being hosed, but his jet-lagged, cheerful compliance — and even enthusiasm — is character-perfect. The escalation of April actually doing it and both of them shrieking is a great physical payoff. The line itself is very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, wake up.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No, five more minutes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We need to go. Now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Fine, fine. I'm up.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're not even awake yet.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes I am. I'm totally awake.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're still lying down.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? Spray me with the hose.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Just spray me with the hose. That'll wake me up.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're inside.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know. Do it anyway.

jokes.text: Ben says he gave Leslie a 'kind nod' as his form of extra support on her last day
jokes.setup: Ann asks everyone to be extra supportive of Leslie on her last day as councilor
jokes.punchline: Ben's idea of going above and beyond is a single 'kind nod' as she walked past
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan from a typically earnest character — the joke works because Ben is Leslie's husband and supposedly her biggest supporter, making the minimalist gesture absurdly funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to spray you with this hose.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes! Do it! I love it!

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'A sorry you lost your dream job gift? That's a tough one. Stay away from wine. Wine is crying juice.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks the group for gift ideas to cheer up Leslie on her last day
jokes.punchline: 'Wine is crying juice' — a perfectly Tom Haverford-style rebranding of something mundane into absurd lifestyle branding
jokes.explanation: Three words: 'Wine is crying juice.' This is classic Tom Haverford — taking a culturally understood truth (women drink wine when sad) and re-labeling it with absurd brand-speak clarity. It's perfectly economical, highly quotable, and couldn't come from any other character. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm already being supportive. I showed up today.

jokes.text: Ben says what Leslie really wants more than anything: 'A nice candle. I'm screwed.'
jokes.setup: The group asks what Leslie really wants more than anything
jokes.punchline: Ben, who knows her best, realizes her deepest desire is a 'nice candle' — making a grand gesture impossible — and immediately sees his problem
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with great economy. The first beat (a nice candle) subverts expectations of something grand, and the immediate self-aware 'I'm screwed' lands the punchline. The joke also characterizes Leslie as someone whose joy comes from small domestic pleasures, which is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Never get Leslie wine. She'll drink the whole bottle and start talking about how she's gonna run for president again.

jokes.text: Councilwoman Ingrid de Forest mentions her 'home away from home is in Zurich — Frank Gehry designed it'
jokes.setup: Leslie shows Ingrid around the City Council chambers, calling it 'your new home away from home'
jokes.punchline: Ingrid casually one-ups with a Frank Gehry-designed home in Zurich, deflating Leslie's civic pride
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for Ingrid as someone absurdly wealthy and casually oblivious about it. The name-dropping of Frank Gehry is specific enough to be funny rather than generic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie wants to make the world a better place. She wants to help people and build meaningful relationships.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh God, that's what everyone wants. I just described every human being. Why would anyone ask that? What am I doing?

jokes.text: Leslie repeatedly fails to complete the sentence 'Today is my last day as a city councilor' — keeps breaking down emotionally
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to deliver a composed speech about her last day
jokes.punchline: She keeps choking on the words and eventually gives up: 'You know what? You get the idea.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating repetition with each attempt cutting off earlier is a good comedic structure — the third attempt being just 'Today is my la--' shows diminishing returns that mirror her emotional state. The final surrender ('You get the idea') is a perfect Leslie-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: City Council chambers is your home away from home.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Well, actually, my home away from home is my architect-designed property in Zurich.

jokes.text: Leslie lists her 'five stages of grief': Denial, anger, Internet commenting, cat adoption, African dance, cat returning to the adoption place, watching all episodes of Murphy Brown, and not giving a flying fart
jokes.setup: Leslie claims she's processed all her feelings and gone through the five stages of grief
jokes.punchline: Her list is both much longer than five and increasingly specific/absurd, culminating in 'not giving a flying fart'
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in escalating list comedy. Each item in the list is funnier than the last, and they follow a loose internal logic (cat adoption → returned the cat) that gives them coherence. 'Internet commenting' as a stage of grief is sharp cultural observation; the Murphy Brown reference shows Leslie's specific cultural world; 'not giving a flying fart' is a perfect kid-friendly Leslie profanity substitute. The payoff question 'How many stages is that?' / 'I don't know. The point is I'm fine now' is a perfect button. Clearly one of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The five stages of grief are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I've identified seven additional stages: negotiating with a higher power you don't believe in, calling your mother, stress-eating an entire rotisserie chicken, Googling 'am I dying,' watching videos of people adopting dogs, considering a complete life overhaul in Costa Rica, and finally, buying a decorative throw pillow that says 'Live, Laugh, Love.'

jokes.text: Ingrid: 'It's like what Sir Ian McKellen said to me the day I sold my boat to Karl Lagerfeld: Parting is such sweet sorrow.' Leslie: 'Oh my God. What is your life?'
jokes.setup: Ingrid tries to console Leslie with a famous quote about parting
jokes.punchline: The quote is attributed to Sir Ian McKellen, in the context of Ingrid casually selling her boat to Karl Lagerfeld — the celebrity name-dropping is so stacked it becomes surreal
jokes.explanation: The joke layers multiple absurdities: Shakespeare being casually quoted in passing, a boat sale to Karl Lagerfeld, a personal friendship with Sir Ian McKellen. Leslie's exasperated 'What is your life?' is the perfect reaction beat — it verbalizes what the audience is thinking, which is a smart comedic choice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There are actually seven stages of grief, not five. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance... and two others I don't remember because I skipped them.

jokes.text: Leslie is caught singing 'Goodbye Yellow Brick Road' out loud without realizing it
jokes.setup: Ingrid approaches Leslie, who seems lost in thought
jokes.punchline: Leslie wasn't speaking, she was singing — and didn't know she was doing it out loud
jokes.explanation: A sweet character beat — the song choice is specifically appropriate (goodbye, yellow brick road) to Leslie's emotional state, making it more earned than a random song. The follow-up where Ingrid offers to harmonize ('I studied opera at the Sorbonne') adds another absurdist character layer.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I'm really going to miss you, Leslie. But hey, look on the bright side – at least you'll finally get to meet Beyoncé.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy, I'm moving to Colorado, not to heaven.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Right, right. Well, when you're there, maybe you'll run into Ryan Gosling at the grocery store or something.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how anything works.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to stay positive. Plus, Oprah's probably in Denver all the time.

jokes.text: Ingrid offers to harmonize with Leslie: 'I studied opera at the Sorbonne. I'd be happy to harmonize.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Ingrid would like to join her in singing
jokes.punchline: Ingrid casually reveals yet another elite credential — Sorbonne opera training — as if it's the most natural thing
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag establishing Ingrid as absurdly overqualified and wealthy. Each revelation is funnier for being delivered with total deadpan earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said, but I'm 87% sure it was insane.

jokes.text: Dr. Saperstein's note to Tom: 'Dear Tom: I win. You suck. Turn note over. You still suck. Turn note over.'
jokes.setup: A lawyer delivers a check and a personal note from Dr. Saperstein to Tom as final payment for Rent-A-Swag
jokes.punchline: The note is juvenile gloating with the 'turn note over' escalation being an unexpectedly petty move from a successful man
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'turn note over' structure is beautifully constructed — we expect the back of the note to have something substantive, but it just repeats 'you still suck.' The willingness of an extremely wealthy man to write this juvenile note reveals his petty character perfectly. High quotability and strong structure justify the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm fine. Everything is fine. I'm just going to go to my office and be fine alone.

jokes.text: Tom tries to convince the lawyer to put a bag of poop in Saperstein's car for $5, negotiates to $10,000, then counter-offers: 'Why don't you just do it for the story?'
jokes.setup: Tom is offended that Saperstein didn't attend the meeting himself
jokes.punchline: Tom's negotiation escalates from $5 to $10,000 before he proposes the lawyer do it 'for the story' — a classic Tom Haverford power move that reveals his total lack of actual leverage
jokes.explanation: The 'for the story' line is a great Tom Haverford-ism — it's exactly the kind of thing someone with his personality and no actual power would say. The escalating negotiation structure works well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love singing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I went to Northwestern. I can teach you.

jokes.text: Ann and Chris: 'That is the most symmetrical fetus I've ever seen. This could be a superhero.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann look at an ultrasound image of their baby
jokes.punchline: Chris's hyperbolic positivity reframes a normal fetus as a potential superhero based on its symmetry
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger — his relentless optimism reframes basic medical information as evidence of extraordinary potential. 'Most symmetrical fetus I've ever seen' establishes he's been studying this, which adds to the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: You're a poopy-head. You're a doo-doo face. You're a buttmunch.

jokes.text: Ben asks how many times the lawyer made Tom turn the note over
jokes.setup: Tom has returned from his meeting; Ben wants to know how the Saperstein note played out
jokes.punchline: Ben's follow-up question implies he was tracking how many times the note said 'turn over,' showing he fully understood the joke of the note — and his 'Oh, that is disappointing' suggests Tom only turned it twice
jokes.explanation: A competent callback that adds a layer to the earlier note joke. 'Oh, that is disappointing' as Ben's reaction implies the note wasn't as long as hoped, which retroactively adds comedy to the original note.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Successful people use money to solve problems.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So I should buy a jet ski?

jokes.text: Ann and Chris hate Dr. Saperstein for destroying Tom's business but love him anyway: 'We love you so much!' / 'I'm loveable!'
jokes.setup: The group acknowledges they 'should hate' Saperstein for what he did to Tom
jokes.punchline: They immediately cave to his charm and declare their love; Saperstein's completely guileless 'I'm loveable!' response makes it even funnier
jokes.explanation: Solid joke about how Saperstein's charisma overrides people's better judgment. The self-confirmation 'I'm loveable!' is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: That'll be $10,000.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, what if I do it for the story?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: For the exposure?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: For the clout?

jokes.text: Ann can't decide whether to find out the baby's sex, cycling through yes/no rapidly, then asks: 'Is there an option other than yes or no?'
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein asks if they want to know the sex of the baby
jokes.punchline: Ann rapidly oscillates between yes and no in the same breath, then asks if there's a third option — suggesting she wants the universe to make this decision for her
jokes.explanation: Functional pregnancy comedy. Ann's anxious indecisiveness is relatable. The 'option other than yes or no' question is amusing but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Look at the symmetry on this one. This kid's gonna be a superhero.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Based on what?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Symmetry. It's the most important thing. Asymmetrical people become villains. It's science.

jokes.text: Ann's pregnancy symptoms deliver three rapid-fire contradictions: 'I have to pee. Wait, no, I have to barf. Wait, no, I have to eat. Actually, all three. Being pregnant is great.'
jokes.setup: The group decides to go eat
jokes.punchline: Ann's body presents conflicting urgent demands simultaneously, and her deadpan 'Being pregnant is great' is a sarcastic button
jokes.explanation: The rapid escalation of bodily needs is well-structured and the deadpan 'Being pregnant is great' lands as ironic understatement. Not wildly original but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: I'm like the most beloved man in this town. Everybody loves me.

jokes.text: Garry/Larry's check is made out to 'Lenny' — 'which I think is a typo for Larry, which isn't even actually my name'
jokes.setup: Tom is distributing proceeds from the Rent-A-Swag sale
jokes.punchline: Larry's check is wrong in two compounding ways — misspelled AND made out to a name that itself was wrong
jokes.explanation: A tight escalation of the show's Larry name gag. The layering — wrong name AND a typo of the wrong name — is good structural comedy. His resigned 'Am I Lenny now?' is a perfect character button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What if we don't find out? We could be surprised.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, there are two options.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, but what if there's a third thing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There's not a third thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But what if science has come up with something new? A third gender baby?

jokes.text: Tom: 'No, it's not, you boring grandpa.' to Larry after Larry says 'Good to be Larry'
jokes.setup: Larry celebrates getting his share of the money
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately deflates Larry's small moment of joy with a specific insult
jokes.explanation: Functional Larry-dunking, which is a show staple. 'Boring grandpa' is specific enough to get a mild laugh but it's not Tom's most creative insult.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm hungry.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm starving. And nauseous. And my feet hurt. And I'm exhausted. And everything smells like pennies. And I think I just felt the baby kick, or maybe I'm just having a stroke. But sure, let's go with pregnancy.

jokes.text: Tom's new investment philosophy: 'For years, I've been coming up with my own ideas. Like some sort of non-rich idiot.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains what he'll do with his $32,000
jokes.punchline: He frames having original ideas as the behavior of a 'non-rich idiot' — inverting the American dream narrative with Tom-logic
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom Haverford line. The phrase 'non-rich idiot' is a perfect Tom-ism — it manages to self-deprecate (he's calling himself an idiot) while also expressing his aspiration (to be rich). The inverted logic (having good ideas is for idiots) is very sharp. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Good to be Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No it's not.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I would wish you the best of luck, but I believe luck is a concept invented by the weak to explain their failures.'
jokes.setup: Tom invites Ron to come hear business pitches with him
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers his philosophy on luck as a substitute for a simple 'good luck'
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson line. The structure subverts a pleasantry by revealing his worldview in a single breath. It sounds like something he's said many times before — deeply held, not performed. The specificity ('invented by the weak to explain their failures') makes it memorable and quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Luck is a concept invented by the weak to explain their failures. I don't believe in luck. I believe in preparation, and I believe in Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Tom on the age-grandfather spectrum: 'Basically, if you're older than me, you're a grandpa. And if you are a grandpa, you're dead.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks if Tom considers everyone here a grandfather
jokes.punchline: Tom's logic escalates: older than Tom = grandpa, grandpa = dead — a logical chain that reveals his solipsistic worldview
jokes.explanation: Tom's logical chain here is very funny — the leap from 'older than me' to 'grandpa' to 'dead' is absurdist but totally consistent with his character. Ron's deadpan 'That sounds right' makes it better.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I was just making observations. First of all, you're not a millennial anymore, you're a geriatric millennial.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then you become a senior millennial, which is basically a boomer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then you're a proto-grandpa.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then you're a full grandpa.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then you're a mega grandpa.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then you're a death grandpa, and that's when you die.

jokes.text: Ben tries to order a 'sad and slow' singing telegram for Leslie, requests something from the Requiem for a Dream soundtrack. The telegram service hangs up.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to find a present for Leslie and calls a singing telegram service
jokes.punchline: His idea of a comforting gift is a 'sad and slow' telegram using music from Requiem for a Dream — a film famous for its brutal, despairing soundtrack — and the service hangs up on him
jokes.explanation: Brilliant, specific joke. The choice of Requiem for a Dream — a film with one of the most harrowing soundtracks in cinema history, associated with addiction and despair — as the right vibe for a sad telegram shows Ben's earnest cluelessness. The singing telegram service hanging up validates the audience's reaction. The specificity of the film reference is what elevates this to 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I got my profit share check!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Jerry. How much?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It says here it's made out to 'Garry Gergich.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not even close to your name.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know! But I've been cashing checks with that name for three years now.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, your actual name is...?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Larry. It's Larry. But everyone calls me Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So your name is Larry, but we call you Jerry, and the government calls you Garry?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Leslie agonizes over potentially having left salt packets at her desk — 'Maybe I should go back for those?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is packing the last of her things from her office
jokes.punchline: Amid the emotional weight of leaving her dream job, she fixates on salt packets as a reason to go back — the mundane specific detail reveals her denial
jokes.explanation: Emotionally true joke — using a mundane object (salt packets) as a proxy for the thing she can't bring herself to say. Ben's gentle 'Honey, there'll be other salt packets' is the perfect straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'd like to order a singing telegram for a funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Telegram Service
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm so sorry for your loss. What song would you like?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Do you have anything from Schindler's List?

jokes.text: Ben: 'Honey, it's okay, there'll be other salt packets. But not the kind that snaps in half, maybe.'
jokes.setup: Leslie worries about the salt packets she left behind
jokes.punchline: Ben reassures her but immediately qualifies — the 'snaps in half' type are indeed special — accidentally validating her anxiety
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic undercutting. Ben tries to be the voice of reason but the qualification ('not the kind that snaps in half, maybe') reveals that he also understands the specific joy of those salt packets, accidentally making Leslie's fixation more reasonable. The 'maybe' hedging is perfectly placed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: There'll be other salt packets.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But will they be *iodized*?

jokes.text: Councilman Dexhart's press conference: 'I totally did all of it.'
jokes.setup: Dexhart holds a press conference saying he's 'here to set the record straight' about inappropriate conduct allegations
jokes.punchline: Rather than denying or minimizing, he simply confirms everything
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection. 'Set the record straight' sets up an expected denial; 'I totally did all of it' is the sharpest possible subversion. The word 'totally' adds casual enthusiasm that makes it even funnier. This is economy at its best — five words do enormous comedic work. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: I've had relations with a woman at Applebee's in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: And I may have Applebee's'd her.

jokes.text: Dexhart: 'I also engaged in inappropriate texting, sexting, and tex-mexting, which is where you send photos of your junk from the restroom of a Chili's To Go.'
jokes.setup: Dexhart continues his confession of inappropriate communications
jokes.punchline: 'Tex-mexting' is a portmanteau coinage that combines texting/sexting/Tex-Mex, and the definition — sending photos from a Chili's To Go restroom — is specific enough to be absurdly funny
jokes.explanation: 'Tex-mexting' is genuinely brilliant coinage — it escalates the existing sexting/texting pattern unexpectedly, and the definition is hyper-specific in a way that grounds the absurdity in a sad, recognizable reality (a Chili's To Go). The word 'junk' combined with 'Chili's' is a deliberately groan-worthy pun bonus. This is one of the episode's top jokes. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: Am I a bad boy?

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: Because I've been very bad and I need to be punished.

jokes.text: Dexhart: 'Another sex scandal? This guy's unbelievable. How does he find the time?'
jokes.setup: Dexhart is confessing to another scandal on the day Leslie is leaving office
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction focuses not on the moral outrage but on the logistical impossibility — how does he physically find the time — which is both funnier and more Leslie
jokes.explanation: A solid character-specific reaction. The 'how does he find the time' framing is funnier than moral indignation because it treats Dexhart's sex life as a scheduling problem.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: I use aliases. Like... Dr. Schlongenberg.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: Or Captain Dong Thunderstick.

dialogue.speaker: Dexhart
dialogue.line: Or... The Penetrator General Von Dongenstein.

jokes.text: Dexhart: 'Does this make me a bad boy? You tell me. No. Really. Tell me. It gets me off when women tell me that.' — and he's reading this from notes
jokes.setup: Dexhart rhetorically asks if his behavior makes him a 'bad boy'
jokes.punchline: What starts as a rhetorical question escalates to a genuine request to be told, then to a sexual admission — and the reveal that this is scripted/written down adds another layer of horror/comedy
jokes.explanation: The escalation from rhetorical → genuine → sexual is very well constructed. The kicker — 'He's reading this, he wrote this down' — is the best possible button, implying he PLANNED to proposition women at his own press conference. The layering of shock and absurdity justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's basically a raccoon shantytown.

jokes.text: Dexhart's pseudonyms: 'Enrique Shockwave, Willie Dynamite, Lee Harvey Teabag, Lieutenant Wilhelm Von Penis'
jokes.setup: Dexhart lists the pseudonyms he used to send inappropriate texts
jokes.punchline: The list escalates in absurdity from vaguely suggestive ('Enrique Shockwave') to political reference with crude pun ('Lee Harvey Teabag') to full military-rank pornographic ('Lieutenant Wilhelm Von Penis')
jokes.explanation: A masterpiece of an escalating list. Each name is funnier and more elaborately crafted than the last. 'Lee Harvey Teabag' is inspired — it uses a historical name as a vessel for crude wordplay in a way that's surprising and structurally elegant. 'Lieutenant Wilhelm Von Penis' reaching full formal military title with a surname that's just the word is the perfect climax. One of the episode's absolute best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so we partner with a local restaurant, right? They give us 20% off appetizers. We take those savings and reinvest them into a premium smoothie line. The smoothie line attracts health-conscious millennials. Those millennials are also interested in cryptocurrency, so we pivot to blockchain consulting. Blockchain consulting leads us naturally into luxury watch repair. And luxury watch repair is just one step away from owning our own clock tower. Clock towers are basically just big Ben. Big Ben is in London. London is where the Royal Family lives. The Royal Family has a lot of money. Money is what we need. Therefore, this plan is foolproof.

jokes.text: The camera or an observer notes: 'He's reading this, he wrote this down.'
jokes.setup: Dexhart has just admitted his arousal confession at the press conference
jokes.punchline: The implication that he scripted and rehearsed this — 'he wrote this down' — makes the absurdity of his prepared admission even more horrifying and funny
jokes.explanation: A great button on the previous joke. 'He wrote this down' adds a layer of premeditation that makes Dexhart's behavior even more absurd — not impulsive, but carefully prepared public sexual confession.

dialogue.speaker: Entrepreneur
dialogue.line: This is going to revolutionize the way people do math. It's a calculator... combined with a vibrator. I call it the 'Calculator.'

jokes.text: Ben interrupts the list with 'Well, at least you won't have to deal with that guy anymore' — as Dexhart continues reading 'Lieutenant Wilhelm Von Penis'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben watch Dexhart's press conference
jokes.punchline: Ben's optimistic silver lining lands simultaneously with the most ridiculous pseudonym on the list, creating comedic counterpoint
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Ben's calm optimism against 'Lieutenant Wilhelm Von Penis' is a well-timed visual/audio joke. Works best on a first viewing when the list's final name lands simultaneously with the reassurance.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A phone-bacus. So you've taken the two least efficient technologies of all time and combined them into one product.

jokes.text: Ben pitches Leslie running against Dexhart with a description that's obviously her but doesn't say her name: 'Someone who is smart and hard-working and who knows the job because she's done it already and is also blond and named Leslie and loves you.'
jokes.setup: Ben suggests someone could beat Dexhart in the next election
jokes.punchline: His clues get increasingly specific ('blond, named Leslie, loves you') before Leslie asks 'Is it you?' — the obvious answer being played straight
jokes.explanation: A classic comedic structure — the over-elaborate hint that leads to an obvious conclusion — executed with warmth. The specific physical descriptors ('blond') elevate it above generic flattery.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I've been thinking about starting a new business venture. It's called 'Rent-A-Swag.' You rent me, and I come to your event and I'm just... swag.

dialogue.speaker: Entrepreneur
dialogue.line: That's the worst idea I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, hear me out. What if we did it backwards? You pay me not to come?

dialogue.speaker: Entrepreneur
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What if I just stood outside your business and looked cool?

dialogue.speaker: Entrepreneur
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What if—

dialogue.speaker: Entrepreneur
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Ben describes Dexhart's district: 'It's basically a dumping ground for old shipping containers. It's like a raccoon shantytown.'
jokes.setup: Ben objects to the plan of spending 51% of their time in Dexhart's district
jokes.punchline: 'A raccoon shantytown' — a specific, evocative image that's both geographically funny and captures Ben's Midwestern pragmatism
jokes.explanation: 'Raccoon shantytown' is a great specific image. The two-part escalation (shipping containers → raccoon shantytown) works well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Did you just sneeze all over this? That's disgusting, man. There's like a million boogers on here.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'So what? I got plenty of dirt on that scumbag. Bring it on.' — cut to cobbled-together banner: 'Second Chunce Four Lesle!'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she's ready to go scorched-earth against Dexhart
jokes.punchline: Her 'professional' campaign materials turn out to be repurposed discarded banners with misspellings — 'Second Chunce Four Lesle'
jokes.explanation: 'Second Chunce Four Lesle' is an inspired misspelling — 'chunce' for 'chance' is the perfect sweet spot of wrong. The title of the episode being a misspelling on a banner is a good meta joke. The contrast between Leslie's confidence and the sad reality of her campaign materials is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Here are some cute girls' names: Emma, Olivia, Sophia...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: And then it just becomes: Broccoli, Cantaloupe, Half a Chicken...

jokes.text: Tom's business pitch process: 'Come on, time is money, money is power, power is pizza, pizza is knowledge. Let's go.'
jokes.setup: Tom tells a pitcher named Greg to skip the chitchat
jokes.punchline: His 'time is money' chain of logic is fine until it hits 'power is pizza' — a logical derailment that reveals his actual priorities
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The chain logic ('time is money, money is power') lulls you with a recognizable pattern, then derails beautifully with 'power is pizza, pizza is knowledge.' The absurdist pivot to pizza AND the reconnection to 'knowledge' (completing the self-help chain) is structurally brilliant. Highly quotable. This is Tom Haverford at his peak. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant and crazy. I will hurt you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But thank you for the offer.

jokes.text: Greg's pitch: 'An abacus, but on your phone. I call it a phone-bacus.' Ron: 'Son, you just described a calculator.'
jokes.setup: Greg pitches his phone app idea with great enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately identifies it as an existing technology; Greg's rejoinder ('but you're talking about it, right?') reveals he understands nothing about business
jokes.explanation: The joke has two good beats: the oblivious pitch AND Greg's PR-brained response to being shot down ('but you're talking about it!') as if buzz is a substitute for innovation. Ron's 'Son...' delivery is perfect paternalistic dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I know he's a terrible person, but I genuinely believe I could fix him. Like, I'm pretty sure all he needs is a good woman and he'd completely turn his life around.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I'm not saying it would be easy, but I think with enough patience and love, I could change him into a decent human being.

jokes.text: Automated Word Counter pitch exchange: 'Three words: Automated word counter. Get out. Two. Words. No. One. Word. As you may know...'
jokes.setup: Another pitcher leads with 'Three words:' and pitches an 'Automated Word Counter'
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'Get out' is met with the pitcher demonstrating his own product by reducing his pitch to progressively fewer words ('Two. Words.' then 'No.' then 'One. Word.') as Tom keeps rejecting him, until he gives up and pivots to a second pitch
jokes.explanation: This is a formally brilliant joke. The pitch for a word counter inadvertently demonstrates itself: three words, then two, then one ('No.') as Tom rejects each attempt. This is self-referential comedy that executes the premise in the delivery. The structure is near-perfect — the joke form and the joke content are the same thing. This is excellent comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, I need business ideas. What do you got?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Poison.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Poison? That's not a business.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It could be. You could poison people, and then sell them the antidote.

jokes.text: Ron announces he'll 'hit the can' during Larry's pitch — Larry then sneezes all over everyone
jokes.setup: Larry is about to pitch his renewable energy idea; Ron announces he needs to use the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Ron's timing is perfect — he escapes just before Larry's massive sneeze covers everyone in the room
jokes.explanation: Ron's instinctive avoidance of Larry's inevitable disaster is a great visual comedy beat. The inferred physical comedy of Larry sneezing 'a gallon of boogers' on everyone is funny, and Tom's 'I'm not gonna buy that thing, it's covered in your boogers' is a great payoff.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm not gonna buy that thing. It's covered in a gallon of your boogers.' Larry: 'I totally understand.'
jokes.setup: Larry sneezes all over his renewable energy prototype
jokes.punchline: Larry's complete acceptance and understanding of being rejected due to his own boogers
jokes.explanation: Larry's defeated 'I totally understand' is perfectly sad. It's a running gag about Larry's complete inability to catch a break, and his resigned acceptance makes it funnier than protest would.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've got a business idea. What if we made a restaurant, but get this... the food was invisible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And people would pay full price, but they'd just be eating air. We'd call it 'The Emperor's Table.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I think we'd make a killing.

jokes.text: Ann listing baby girl names: 'Daisy, Annabelle, Lilly. Olive, rosemary, chicken. Fifty burritos.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Chris discuss how great it would be to have a girl; Ann lists cute girl names
jokes.punchline: Her list of names slides from normal names to herbs to a food item to a food quantity — she's been overtaken by pregnancy hunger mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The gradual transition from names to herbs (Olive, Rosemary — which are ALSO names, creating ambiguity) to 'Chicken' to 'Fifty burritos' is structurally perfect — you don't realize she's lost the thread until 'chicken' and it fully pays off with 'fifty burritos.' The immediacy of her then flagging down the server validates it. The joke earns 8+ for its elegant structure and perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made a campaign banner from recycled materials I found behind the community center. It says 'Lesli Knope for City Council: We Can Do This Together' — wait, why does it say 'Lesli'? And what does 'Garbageman Forever' mean? That's not even... oh God, I think I glued newspaper clippings upside down.

jokes.text: Ann threatens the server: 'I'm pregnant and I'm a little bit crazy. So if you don't bring our appetizers out in the next 30 seconds, I'm gonna plunge your face into the deep fryer!' — followed immediately by: 'And also two waters, please. But no hurry. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Ann is extremely hungry and tries to get the server's attention
jokes.punchline: The extreme threat (face in deep fryer) is immediately followed by the polite, apologetic request (two waters, no hurry, thank you) — the whiplash between menace and politeness is the joke
jokes.explanation: The structure here is near-perfect — the escalating threat is already funny, but the instant pivot to 'And also two waters, please. But no hurry. Thank you' is brilliant misdirection. The 'But no hurry' after threatening violence captures the genuine contradiction of pregnant-hunger anxiety perfectly. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to have a boy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Chris!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know. I've been picturing it — me and my son, playing catch in the backyard, teaching him about nutrition and self-improvement.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why? What's disturbing about that?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't know, the image of you in shorts throwing a ball around.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, that's not going to stop me. I'm still going to do it.

jokes.text: Dexhart's poll numbers are up since the scandal because people found out he was Miley Cyrus' cousin
jokes.setup: A reporter tells Leslie that Dexhart's poll numbers are actually up despite the scandal
jokes.punchline: The reason for the popularity boost is unrelated to politics — he's Miley Cyrus' cousin
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical joke about voter logic — a sex scandal is irrelevant next to celebrity proximity. The specific 'Miley Cyrus' (relevant to 2013 when this aired) makes it land harder as a cultural observation.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't read this. What does this say? Is that a... is that a foot? Or a... or a butt?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's definitely a foot.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, I don't know! I've never seen an ultrasound before. For all I know, the baby could be a blob.

jokes.text: Shauna Malwae-Tweep reads Dexhart's text 'Sweet jugs' — then admits 'He's kinda cute. I feel like I could fix him, you know?'
jokes.setup: Leslie shares evidence of Dexhart's inappropriate texts
jokes.punchline: Shauna, a journalist who should be outraged, is instead charmed — and her 'I could fix him' rationalization is a pointed observational joke
jokes.explanation: 'I feel like I could fix him' is a recognizable and satirically pointed rationalization. Leslie's 'Oh God, Shauna, no' is the correct reaction. Solid joke that lands on a real human truth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm running for City Council!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: [complete silence]

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So that's a yes from everyone. Great! I can feel the energy in this room.

jokes.text: April's business idea: 'Macaroni and poison. It's like mac and cheese, but with a special ingredient.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks his team to pitch ideas since all outside pitches failed
jokes.punchline: April's idea is mac and cheese but poisoned — delivered with complete sincerity as a business proposition
jokes.explanation: Absolutely April. The framing of poison as a 'special ingredient' is brilliantly deadpan, and the phrase 'macaroni and poison' works as a product name. This could ONLY be April Ludgate — no other character on television would pitch a poisoned food product as a sincere business idea. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Look, I want to tell you to just wing it and embrace the chaos, but I know that's terrible advice. So instead I'm going to tell you the responsible thing: make a detailed plan, stick to it, and don't deviate. Also, I'm lying. Wing it. Chaos is fun.

jokes.text: Ron's business idea: expanding socket sets to include sizes up to 5/8 inch
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron for a business idea
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'big idea' is an extremely specific, practical, unglamorous socket set expansion — delivered with the same gravity as others might pitch world-changing technology
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. His practical, tactile, utterly unglamorous 'idea' is funny because of the context (a startup pitch session) and the seriousness with which he delivers it. The specificity of '5/8 inch' makes it funnier than a vague answer would. Justifies 8+ for character integration alone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're going to do great in this campaign. You just need to believe in yourself and remember why you're doing this in the first place.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Also, I've been stealing office supplies for three years and I think someone finally noticed because Jerry asked me about my stapler yesterday.

jokes.text: Andy's business idea: 'Bears bouncing on trampoline roads. There's a chance I might have dreamed that.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks a jet-lagged Andy for a business idea
jokes.punchline: Andy pitches 'bears bouncing on trampoline roads' and then acknowledges he may have dreamed it — his uncertainty about whether he was awake when he had this idea is the extra beat
jokes.explanation: An excellent joke that also serves as a callback to the jet lag plot. 'Bears bouncing on trampoline roads' is perfect Andy — genuinely delightful rather than just dumb, and the self-aware 'I might have dreamed that' is a superb button. The uncertainty about the boundary between his dreams and waking life connects back to his jet lag. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't just run for office. It requires strategy, patience, and a willingness to compromise your principles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you're a big stupid butt, Ron!

jokes.text: Larry: 'I've missed an entire day of work, so at least some good came from this.'
jokes.setup: The pitch session has been a failure; the group prepares to leave
jokes.punchline: Larry finds the silver lining — missing work — which reveals that his job is something he'd rather avoid
jokes.explanation: A nice quiet joke — Larry's resigned contentment at missing work is both self-deprecating and a little sad. Clean delivery.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're upset because I'm more successful than you. I have a better job, I make more money, I have better health insurance, my car is newer, my apartment is nicer, I've read more books, I've been to more countries, I speak more languages, my skin is clearer, I'm taller, I'm faster, I'm stronger, and I'm significantly better looking.

jokes.text: The second banner read: 'Perv Dexxxhrt equals... birthday mouse'
jokes.setup: Leslie's patched-together campaign banner has a second section
jokes.punchline: 'Birthday mouse' — assembled from random discarded banners, the anti-Dexhart message becomes incomprehensible, and 'birthday mouse' has no explanation
jokes.explanation: 'Birthday mouse' is delightfully random and the correction ('Rat! That's the closest thing I could get to a rat!') makes it even better — Leslie had a plan, and the plan included a rat, and the rat became a birthday mouse. The episode title callback gives this extra resonance.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm the Deputy Director of the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're the only one in the Parks Department.

jokes.text: Leslie corrects the banner: 'Rat! That's the closest thing I could get to a rat.' The rat on the banner is a birthday mouse.
jokes.setup: Ben reads the banner as 'birthday mouse'
jokes.punchline: Leslie explains it's supposed to be a rat and the birthday mouse was the closest she could find — implying she searched through available banner graphics for a rat
jokes.explanation: The explanation makes it funnier — 'birthday mouse' wasn't accidental, it was the BEST SHE COULD DO. The image of Leslie searching through banner clipart for a rat and settling on a birthday mouse is very funny. Good payoff on the banner visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Talking Tissue
dialogue.line: You can do it!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It really works!

jokes.text: Chris reveals he perfected shaving the human face and wants to pass it on, then mentions 'tiny little acorn penis' as a pro of having a boy
jokes.setup: Chris is excited about the prospect of having a boy and listing the things he could share
jokes.punchline: 'Tiny little acorn penis' as the final item on the list of father-son bonding activities is a jarring but affectionate detail that Chris adds with complete earnestness; Ben's reaction ('A weird image. But one that does not diminish my enthusiasm.') is the button
jokes.explanation: Chris's guileless enthusiasm transforms what could be an awkward moment into something sweet and funny. The phrase 'tiny little acorn penis' is maximally specific and disarming. Ben's diplomatic response ('A weird image. But one that does not diminish my enthusiasm.') is a perfectly structured reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Hey baby, what's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: That's cool, that's cool. So what do you say we get out of here?

jokes.text: Chris: 'Tiny little acorn penis? Forget it.' then self-corrects: 'A weird image. But one that does not diminish my enthusiasm.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann discuss wanting a boy; Chris lists the joys of raising a son
jokes.punchline: Chris's list of delights includes 'tiny little acorn penis' — he catches himself, acknowledges it's a weird image, but refuses to let it dampen his enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'tiny little acorn penis' is unexpected enough to get a big laugh, and the callback-to-self ('a weird image, but one that does not diminish my enthusiasm') is a perfect Chris Traeger self-correction. His inability to let even his own awkward phrasings dampen his optimism is quintessential Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I'm very open-minded. I call 'em like I see 'em. Ann, you're beautiful. Chris, you're beautiful.

jokes.text: The sealed baby sex envelope is opened and the note is completely illegible: 'I... leg smurf.' / 'Are we having a smurf?' / 'We are having a... 11-jewel toilet.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Chris open the doctor's sealed envelope to find out the baby's sex
jokes.punchline: Saperstein's handwriting is so bad the note is unreadable — producing nonsense phrases that get increasingly absurd ('11-jewel toilet')
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of the misread text — from plausibly medical ('I... leg') to 'smurf' to '11-jewel toilet' — is well-structured. The question 'Are we having a smurf?' is a great delivery. The escalation of nonsense before the real reveal creates good sustained comedic tension.

dialogue.speaker: Saperstein's son
dialogue.line: Dad, the TV is broken. It keeps showing these weird channels.

dialogue.speaker: Saperstein's son
dialogue.line: Well, I was looking for ESPN, but I accidentally hit some buttons and now there's all these... instructional videos.

dialogue.speaker: Saperstein's son
dialogue.line: They're about, um, physical education. Very physical. And there's a lot of heavy breathing.

dialogue.speaker: Saperstein's son
dialogue.line: The people in them aren't wearing much, and they keep calling me 'son' which is weird because you're the only one supposed to call me that.

dialogue.speaker: Saperstein's son
dialogue.line: Oh, and I may have used your credit card to unlock the premium channels. I thought it would fix the malfunction.

jokes.text: We are having a... 'distributions.' / That's what it looks like: Distributions. / Let me see that. / It says 'congratulations,' I think. / Then it says, 'I... leg smurf.' / Are we having a smurf?
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein sealed the baby's sex in an envelope with a handwritten note. Now they're trying to read his terrible handwriting.
jokes.punchline: His handwriting is so bad that 'congratulations' becomes 'distributions,' and the sex reveal becomes 'I leg smurf,' prompting Chris to ask if they're 'having a smurf.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating unreadability of the note builds beautifully, and each misread is funnier than the last. 'Are we having a smurf?' is a perfect moment of Chris's earnestness meeting absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: How are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Oh, you know, same old same old. My mom's been seeing this guy who's... well, let's just say he's closer to my age than hers.

jokes.text: Ann, deeply stressed about not knowing the baby's sex: 'I'm calling Domino's. Do you think Domino's delivers to this restaurant?'
jokes.setup: The group is stressed about not being able to read the sex note; Chris calls the doctor
jokes.punchline: Ann's response to extreme stress is to call Domino's pizza — and ask whether they deliver to another restaurant
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of 'do you think Domino's delivers to this restaurant?' elevates it from a basic hunger joke to an absurdist one — she's already at a restaurant but needs more food from a different restaurant. Good character integration with the pregnancy hunger theme.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've implemented a new dramatic entrance policy. From now on, I burst through doors like I'm about to deliver life-changing news.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It makes me seem more important and keeps people on their toes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus, it's great for my personal brand.

jokes.text: Leslie announces her campaign and says: 'Oh, I love the sound of silence before a big cheer.' — then 'That's what's happening, right?'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces her plan to run for Dexhart's seat to her colleagues
jokes.punchline: No one cheers; Leslie interprets the silence as anticipatory, then reality-checks herself
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured cringe beat. 'I love the sound of silence before a big cheer' is an inspired rationalization — it's the kind of thing Leslie would genuinely think AND say. The follow-up 'That's what's happening, right?' is the perfect crack in her confidence. This is Leslie Knope at her most human and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Talking Tissue
dialogue.line: You've got this, buddy! Now blow your nose, champ!

dialogue.speaker: Talking Tissue
dialogue.line: Feeling better? Of course you are, because you're a winner!

dialogue.speaker: Talking Tissue
dialogue.line: Remember that time you almost asked out Jennifer? Me too. You blew it, pal.

dialogue.speaker: Talking Tissue
dialogue.line: But hey, there's always tomorrow! Unless you get sick again. Then it's just tissues and regret.

jokes.text: April: 'I would love it if you ran an insane campaign and basically turned into the Joker. But that means you probably shouldn't do it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April for her honest opinion on running again
jokes.punchline: April's honest feedback acknowledges she WANTS the chaos of Leslie going full villain, and uses that desire as her reason to recommend against it
jokes.explanation: Pure April Ludgate. The joke works on two levels: it's honest advice delivered in the most April way possible (she'd genuinely enjoy Leslie's unraveling), and the logic is impeccable in its April-ness — her desire for chaos IS a warning sign. 'Basically turned into the Joker' is an inspired characterization. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: The reason that terrible people seem to win is because good people assume the worst won't happen. They don't prepare for it. Terrible people, on the other hand, they're always ready. They're always planning. I once knew a man who tried to take over the Virgin Islands with a real estate empire.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I don't know, Leslie. It seems risky. But I could be wrong. I haven't pooped in three days.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asked his opinion on Leslie's campaign plan
jokes.punchline: He qualifies his own judgment by noting he hasn't pooped in three days — as if this is a relevant epistemic disclosure
jokes.explanation: The jet lag callback makes this earned rather than random. The structure of 'I could be wrong. I haven't pooped in three days' treats constipation as a legitimate caveat to his judgment, which is such an Andy-specific form of self-awareness. Among the most quotable lines in the episode. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: You know what the secret to success is? You gotta find a mentor. Someone older, wiser, who can guide you through life.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Build a relationship with them. Spend time together. Get to know them on a personal level.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: And if they're your high school teacher, well, even better. The dynamics are already there.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I do not think you should run again.' Leslie: 'What the hell do you know, Dum-Dum?'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron for his sage counsel, saying his words carry great influence
jokes.punchline: He tells her not to run; she immediately dismisses him as 'Dum-Dum'
jokes.explanation: The setup is the classic Leslie Knope move — earnestly seeking wise counsel and then immediately ignoring it when it's not what she wants to hear. The word 'Dum-Dum' coming from Leslie — who so rarely insults anyone she respects — makes it even funnier. The structure (she builds it up, gets the answer, immediately dismisses it) is very tight. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: You should really trust my advice on this.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: I'm going to be brutally honest with you: I don't care about you at all.

jokes.text: Ingrid immediately and enthusiastically endorses Leslie's bad idea: 'Leslie, you're running for office again? What a great idea! How can I help?'
jokes.setup: Everyone has just told Leslie her plan is bad; she declares she's running anyway
jokes.punchline: Ingrid, the only person who hasn't weighed in, bursts in with pure enthusiasm — having missed the entire conversation
jokes.explanation: Functional joke playing on the dramatic irony of the situation — Ingrid's naive enthusiasm directly contradicts the consensus everyone just reached. The 'Ugh...' from Leslie/group lands the reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Jen, I know your hourly rate is very expensive, so I'll keep this brief.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But I just wanted to say how much I appreciate everything you've done, and I think you're really great, and—

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's going to cost you $500.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? For what?

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: For me listening to you talk. You owe me money for every word you say.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God, okay, okay. I'm done. Bye, Jen. You're the best!

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: That's $50,000. I'm suing you.

jokes.text: Tom's Talking Tissue product: 'Blow that nose, playah!'
jokes.setup: Tom gives up waiting for good pitches and invents his own product: a talking tissue that hypes you up
jokes.punchline: The demo message is 'Blow that nose, playah!' — hyping you up to do the most mundane thing
jokes.explanation: 'Blow that nose, playah!' perfectly captures Tom's brand voice — it's motivational content applied to the most anticlimactic possible action. The subsequent messages later in the episode extend the joke well.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We don't care if it's a boy or a girl. We just want a healthy baby.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Exactly. Gender is completely irrelevant to us.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Although, a boy would be nice.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, a boy would be great.

jokes.text: Larry being told his same job: 'I'm younger than you, and I already have my own department. Plus I'm married, and I make more money than you.'
jokes.setup: Tom sympathizes with Larry being stuck in the same job
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'sympathy' consists of listing all the ways he's already surpassed Larry — it's the most Tom Haverford version of commiseration
jokes.explanation: A Tom and Larry dynamic joke — Tom's competitive instinct overrides any actual sympathy. Solid character work, not a showstopper.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Chris and Ann, you two are going to make wonderful parents. In fact, I'd like to offer my own children for adoption. They're adults now, so there shouldn't be any legal issues. Jerry's a disappointment, Millicent's a bigger disappointment, and Craig... well, Craig's in prison.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Whatever. You just merged your department with parks then made up your own title.' Tom: 'Yeah. It's awesome.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to push back on Tom's bragging
jokes.punchline: Tom completely agrees with Larry's critique without any shame — confirming it WAS a power move and it WAS awesome
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete lack of defensiveness is the joke — Larry expected pushback and got agreement. Tom's shameless self-satisfaction ('Yeah. It's awesome.') is great character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: Well, I'm Perd Hapley, and I just witnessed a press conference. What happened at the press conference? A woman spoke. What did the woman do? She pressed. What did she press? Matters. Were there members of the press there? Yes, there were, and that's why it was called a press conference.

jokes.text: Talking Tissue: 'I'm empty, yo. Fill me up.' / 'Do that again.'
jokes.setup: Tom demonstrates the Talking Tissue product
jokes.punchline: The tissue dispenser says 'I'm empty, yo. Fill me up.' — a hyper-motivational voice for a completely mundane task; Tom's 'Do that again' shows his own delight
jokes.explanation: Good running extension of the Talking Tissue gag. 'I'm empty, yo. Fill me up.' continues the brand voice and 'Do that again' shows Tom has already become his own biggest customer.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio tries to hit on Ann: 'What do you say you and I get together in a special way?' Ann: 'I'm pregnant.' Jean-Ralphio: 'The more the merrier.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio appears at Dr. Saperstein's house early in the morning
jokes.punchline: Ann's pregnancy doesn't deter him — 'the more the merrier' — treating the baby as a bonus rather than an obstacle
jokes.explanation: Classic Jean-Ralphio — completely undeterred by any social signal. 'The more the merrier' as a response to pregnancy is perfectly in character and gets a good laugh.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio tries to hit on Chris too: 'Well, you can come too, beautiful.' Chris thanks him. Jean-Ralphio: 'Look at that. I guess sometimes I call men beautiful too. I guess I'm open-minded as hell.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio realizes he's also called Chris 'beautiful'
jokes.punchline: His reaction is to frame his own slip as evidence of his open-mindedness — delivered with total self-congratulation
jokes.explanation: 'I guess I'm open-minded as hell' is a great Jean-Ralphio line — it turns an accidental moment into a self-compliment, which is quintessential Jean-Ralphio. The casual 'I guess' makes it funnier. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio deflects from the TV's porno ordering: 'Also, there's a malfunction with the TV where it keeps ordering porno. Like, a ton of porno. Like, how can someone watch that much porno in one sitting? Only when you're out of the house. So if you see it on the bill, that's why. Okay?'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is saying goodbye as Dr. Saperstein leaves for the day
jokes.punchline: His 'malfunction' explanation immediately contradicts itself — 'only when you're out of the house' — confessing while attempting to cover
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-incrimination is well-constructed — Jean-Ralphio keeps adding details that undermine his own excuse, including the fatal tell 'only when you're out of the house.' The delivery is key: he says this to his father. Very Jean-Ralphio.

jokes.text: Jen Barkley on Ben spending her consultation time on pleasantries: 'I get paid $1,200 an hour. Do you really want to spend any of that time talking about my mother and her 19-year-old Korean husband?'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how Jen is doing and how her family is
jokes.punchline: Jen's deflection reveals a deeply complicated home life — her mother has a 19-year-old Korean husband — dropped as casually as a billing rate
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it characterizes Jen as someone who has no time for niceties, reveals an absurd family situation with total non-reaction, and uses the billing rate framing to make the personal revelation feel transactional. The specific detail of '19-year-old Korean husband' is maximally funny in its specificity. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron bursts through the door dramatically: 'RON!' — Leslie: 'That's how I enter rooms now. It's more dramatic.' Ron: 'Why did you enter at all?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Jen are in the middle of a private consultation
jokes.punchline: Ron has adopted the habit of announcing his own entrance by saying his own name dramatically; Leslie's 'why did you enter at all?' is the straight-man response
jokes.explanation: Ron announcing himself by shouting his own name is a perfect absurdist character gag — it's something Ron would unilaterally decide is appropriate and refuse to explain or defend. 'That's how I enter rooms now. It's more dramatic' is delivered with total Ron Swanson conviction. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to the Talking Tissue: 'Yo, dog! Life is what you make of it.' Ron: 'Leave while I'm ahead? You got it.'
jokes.setup: Tom demonstrates the Talking Tissue to Ron after pitching his business liaison idea
jokes.punchline: Ron hears one motivational tissue message and immediately decides to leave — the contrast between the hype-speak and Ron's austere personality makes his departure the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is Ron taking the tissue's message as a literal directive to leave. His complete, unironic compliance ('You got it') is perfect Ron. Good running gag payoff.

jokes.text: Talking Tissue extended sequence: 'Clear them sinuses, playboy!' / 'Someone's got the sniffies.' / 'Tell your mama you love 'er.' / 'Step up your vitamin C game, bro!'
jokes.setup: The Talking Tissue keeps dispensing messages
jokes.punchline: The messages escalate from nose-specific to general health advice to relationship advice — the product scope creep is funny
jokes.explanation: 'Tell your mama you love 'er' as a tissue message is wonderfully off-mission. The escalation from nose health to maternal relationships to vitamin supplements shows Tom's product has no coherent brand strategy — which is itself the joke.

jokes.text: Jen Barkley: 'I should know. Those terrible people have paid me so much money, I have a condo in every virgin island.'
jokes.setup: Jen tells Leslie that terrible people defeat great people all the time
jokes.punchline: She has personal financial evidence — she's been paid by terrible people to defeat great people so many times she owns property in every US Virgin Island
jokes.explanation: 'A condo in every virgin island' is a great specific flex — not 'every island,' specifically 'every VIRGIN island,' which is both geographically specific and funny. It characterizes Jen as someone who has profited enormously from doing morally questionable work without apology.

jokes.text: Jen's advice metaphor: 'Don't be the kid that graduates high school, hangs out in the school parking lot. Be the woman who moves away, climbs the ladder, and then confidently comes back and has sex with her hot old English teacher just for kicks.'
jokes.setup: Jen is advising Leslie not to stay small by running for local office again
jokes.punchline: The inspirational metaphor pivots from conventional self-improvement advice to a very specific sexual conquest as the ultimate symbol of confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best speeches. The metaphor starts recognizably, pivots unexpectedly to sleeping with an English teacher, and the pivot is completely consistent with Jen's character — power and success expressed through unabashed personal pleasure. The follow-up revelation ('Is that what you did?' 'Yeah. Mr. Baker. Sex was pretty good, thanks to me.') makes it even better by confirming it was a direct autobiography. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Is that what you did?' Jen: 'Yeah. Mr. Baker. Sex was pretty good, thanks to me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Jen actually did what she described in her metaphor
jokes.punchline: Jen confirms it literally happened, names the teacher, and adds the characteristically self-confident assessment that the sex was good 'thanks to me'
jokes.explanation: 'Sex was pretty good, thanks to me' is a masterclass in character-specific line writing — the 'thanks to me' is pure Jen Barkley, claiming credit even for mutual activity, completely unbothered. The casualness of 'Mr. Baker' naming the teacher elevates the joke. Strong candidate for best line of the episode.

jokes.text: Jen: 'because I don't care enough about you to lie.'
jokes.setup: Jen tells Leslie she can trust her advice
jokes.punchline: The reason she can be trusted is not warmth or loyalty but indifference — she has no investment in Leslie's feelings
jokes.explanation: The single best line in the episode. Nine words that perfectly encapsulate Jen Barkley's character, invert the expected reassurance structure, and work as both a laugh line AND genuinely wise advice. The joke IS the wisdom — honesty through apathy is a real thing, and Jen delivers it with perfect deadpan. Maximum economy (could not be shorter), perfect character integration (no other character could say this), and the structure is a masterpiece of misdirection. The setup ('you can trust me...') leads you toward warmth and pivots to cold logic. This is the calibration anchor for this episode.

jokes.text: Jen's billing clock runs out mid-conversation: 'Okay, if you want to keep talking, you're gonna have to pay me $1,200 more dollars. I swear to God, if you say one more word, you will legally owe me $1,200, and I will sue you. Let's not end it like that.'
jokes.setup: Jen's hour of consulting time runs out
jokes.punchline: Jen immediately shifts to legal threats while also trying to wrap up graciously — the coexistence of warmth ('let's not end it like that') and threat ('I will sue you') is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good character work — Jen's professional ruthlessness coexisting with a desire to end on pleasant terms is funny and consistent. 'Those five words are on me' for 'Great to see you, Leslie' is a nice button.

jokes.text: Dr. Saperstein: 'Would you be interested in adopting my children? They're in their late 20s, they're terrible. No? No go? I ask all my patients.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein has just delivered the happy news about the baby's sex
jokes.punchline: He uses the warm moment to try to offload his adult children, adding 'I ask all my patients' which makes it somehow worse
jokes.explanation: Extraordinary joke. The layers: his children are adults, he's trying to give them away, he describes them as 'terrible,' his fall-back 'No go?' is dejected, and the reveal that 'I ask all my patients' is standard practice makes it much darker and funnier. The joke tells us everything we need to know about Jean-Ralphio's upbringing. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'big announcement' turns out to be going to lunch with her husband, eating waffles, then making out on the couch
jokes.setup: Leslie has gathered everyone for a 'very big announcement about her future'
jokes.punchline: The announcement is lunch at JJ's diner and waffles — a massive comedic undercut of the solemn atmosphere
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is very well set up — the solemn gathering, the pause, the formal language of 'a very big announcement.' The payoff (waffles and couch makeout) works because it's perfectly Leslie: her authentic 'big plans' are domestic joy. The structure is clean and the character integration is excellent. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley: 'There you have it. A shockingly unshocking press conference in which a recently unemployed woman said nothing of importance. I'm Perd Hapley, and I just realized I'm not holding my microphone.'
jokes.setup: Perd Hapley delivers his closing summary of Leslie's non-announcement press conference
jokes.punchline: His summary is a tautology ('shockingly unshocking') and he finishes by realizing he forgot his microphone — the incompetence extends to the reporter covering the non-story
jokes.explanation: A great Perd Hapley moment. 'Shockingly unshocking' is perfect Perd-speak — a redundant construction that sounds analytical but means nothing. The microphone revelation is a perfect button showing Perd's ongoing incompetence as a journalist. Justifies 8+ for the combination of character-specific verbal tics and the physical comedy button.

jokes.text: Leslie's monologue: '...and if you have the ability to go to Paris, by all means, go to Paris!'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers an earnest speech about finding peace in times of transition
jokes.punchline: The solemn advice pivots to a very specific travel recommendation — and then she's immediately in Paris
jokes.explanation: The tonal pivot from solemn advice to specific travel tip is a well-executed misdirection that sets up the Paris reveal. The enthusiasm of 'by all means, go to Paris!' after the generic self-help language is a good beat.

jokes.text: Ben's surprise gift for Leslie turns out to be Paris
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie her real present 'isn't here, we have to go get it' — the camera pulls back to reveal a plane taking off
jokes.punchline: He has taken her to Paris — the ultimate fulfillment of the episode's theme that she should 'go bigger'
jokes.explanation: More of an emotional beat than a pure comedy moment, but the reveal works comedically through the callback to the episode's themes and the misdirection of 'we have to go get it.' The monologue setup ('if you have the ability to go to Paris, by all means go to Paris') is a good comedic undercut before the reveal.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben both face new challenges on the first day of new jobs. Donna, April and Andy play a prank on Ben, while Tom prepares for a big presentation. Meanwhile Ann and Chris contemplate taking a big leap together.
insight: 66 jokes in 27 minutes but escalation-driven absurdism keeps impact modest at 6.61.
